anchor.quote: The full citation gives users detail they might need

Most government writing about cases requires a full citation. Citations show people where to find the published authorised judgments and decisions of courts, commissions and tribunals. They also tell people who made the decision and what year it was made.
Citations can be in text or in notes, depending on organisational style and the format of the content.

anchor.quote: Decisions are either reported or unreported
Reported decisions are published in authorised law reports (a report series). For example:
Unreported decisions are published in report series from the legal authorities themselves. For example:

The abbreviations for the report series of reported and unreported decisions are different. Some unreported decisions are published in a report series later on. This is why the same case might have 2 or more citations.
The authorised report of a case might have been published some time after the decision was handed down.

not_rules.note: Background note explaining discrepancy in dates.

anchor.quote: Civil and criminal case titles have different elements
Civil and criminal cases have specific citation elements. They differ.
In civil case titles, the ‘v’ is pronounced ‘and’. In criminal case titles, the ‘v’ is pronounced ‘against’.

not_rules.note: Pronunciation guidance; does not affect written text.

anchor.quote: Civil cases usually involve a dispute between organisations or individuals. The plaintiff is the person or organisation who files a complaint with the court. The other party is the defendant.
Most citations use only family names. Corporation names are usually given in full, although abbreviations are acceptable.
‘Re’ means ‘in the matter of’ and that is how it is said. ‘Re’ in the title of a civil case means the court acts in a particular way – for example, in an advisory capacity.
‘Ex parte’ means an application brought before the court by one party without the other party having to be notified – for example, when one party applies for an injunction.
Criminal cases are usually initiated by the Commonwealth or state (for the Crown) against people or organisations (the defendants) who are alleged to have committed an offence under criminal law.
Decisions can differ between judges or magistrates

Most tribunals are established by Acts of parliament which set out their powers, functions and operations. Acts give tribunals the legal authority to make decisions. There are tribunals in each state and territory.
Under the Constitution, only federal courts have the judicial power of the Commonwealth. Commonwealth tribunals exercise administrative rather than judicial power.
Federal courts cannot review administrative decisions made by government, so parliament often gives this power to a tribunal.
The president and members of a tribunal can be judges. For example, the President of the Administrative Appeals Tribunal is a judge of the Federal Court of Australia.
Find the decision title on the tribunal website or an alternative

anchor.quote: Decisions are published on tribunal websites, on the Federal Court of Australia’s website or on AustLII.
There are a large number of Commonwealth tribunals, including:
The AAT has an authorised report series – the Administrative Law Decisions (ALD). The AAT’s unauthorised report series, AATA, is available on AustLII.
The Fair Work Commission also has an authorised report series – the Industrial Reports (IR). Unauthorised reports are available on the commission’s website.
The Commissioner of Taxation has the power to make rulings – public, private and oral – that interpret the laws administered by the Australian Taxation Office (ATO).
Public rulings comprise rulings and determinations and are legally binding advice. Draft and final public rulings are published on the ATO Legal Database.

rules.quote:
The full titles of public rulings have 3 elements that appear in a set order:
1. a ruling or determination type – for example, ‘Goods and Services Tax Ruling’
2. a number – for example, ‘GSTR 2019/1’
3. a title in italics – for example, Goods and services tax: supply of anything other than goods or real property connected with the indirect tax zone (Australia).

examples.note: Crown as appellant written as 'The Queen'

parts.quote: The Queen v Baden-Clay [2016] HCA 35

tags.violation_condition: Using 'R' instead of 'The King' (or 'The Queen') in criminal appeals, or placing parties in the wrong order

when: In criminal appeals involving the Crown
rules.why: G-2: Specific rule governing the naming of the Crown in criminal appeals.

anchor.quote: When citing cases using notes, always use a full citation as the first citation. After that, you can use the name of the first party, followed by the case citation.

covers.quote: Subsequent citations in notes use the first party

examples.note: Full citation first time in notes

parts.quote: 1 Steinmetz v Shannon(2019) 99 NSWLR 687. [The full citation the first time]

examples.note: Subsequent note citation using first party

parts.quote: 8 Steinmetz (2019) 99 NSWLR 687. [Only the first party to the case in a subsequent note]

tags.violation_condition: Using a short citation on first mention in notes, or omitting the case citation after the first party in subsequent note citations

when: When citing cases in notes
rules.why: G-4: Explains full vs short form note citation rules.

anchor.quote: If you use notes, write pinpoint page numbers for the citation using ‘at [page number]’.

covers.quote: You can follow the page number with the number of the relevant paragraph as it appears in the judgment. Write the paragraph number in square brackets.
Use a comma to list separate pinpoint citations.
Pinpoint citations use ‘at’ for page and paragraph numbers

examples.note: Pinpoint using 'at [page number]'

parts.quote: 1Ruddock v Vadarlis (2001) 110 FCR 491 at 1191. [The pinpoint citation is on page 1191.]

examples.note: Pinpoint with paragraph in square brackets and comma separation

parts.quote: 2Rojoda Pty Ltd v Commissioner of State Revenue (2018) 368 ALR 734 at 737 [10], 760 [108]. [The pinpoint citations are at page 737 (paragraph 10) and page 760 (paragraph 108).]

tags.violation_condition: Pinpoint citation in notes without 'at' before page number, or with incorrect paragraph bracket syntax

when: When writing pinpoint citations in notes
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Consolidates pinpoint citation formatting in notes.

anchor.quote: Identify the judicial officer whose judgment you are citing. Cite the case fully and add ‘per [name] [judicial office abbreviation]’.

covers.quote: Use these abbreviations:

examples.note: Using 'per [name] [abbreviation]'

parts.quote: UBS AG v Tyne (2018) 92 ALJR 968 at 979 [45] per Kiefel CJ, Bell and Keane JJ, [61] per Gageler J.

examples.note: Using 'per Deane and Gaudron JJ'

parts.quote: Mabo v Queensland [No 2] (1992) 175 CLR 1 at 106–107 per Deane and Gaudron JJ.

tags.violation_condition: Citing a specific judicial officer's judgment without 'per [name] [abbreviation]'

when: When citing the judgment of a specific judicial officer
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Rule specifying formula for citing individual judicial officers.

anchor.quote: Write the title of all tribunal decisions in italics.

covers.quote: Titles for Commonwealth tribunal decisions are in italics

examples.note: Tribunal decision title formatted in italics

parts.quote: Application by Flexigroup Limited [2020] ACompT 1 [Australian Competition Tribunal decision]

tags.violation_condition: A tribunal decision title not set in italics

when: For titles of Commonwealth tribunal decisions
rules.why: G-4: Core typographic requirement for tribunal decision titles.

anchor.quote: Use an initial capital when you refer to specific rulings.

covers.quote: For subsequent mentions, write the type of ruling or determination or write the number.
Specify whether it’s a ruling or determination in all subsequent mentions

examples.note: Capitalised 'Ruling' referring to a specific ruling

parts.quote: ‘the Ruling’

examples.note: Capitalised 'Determination' referring to a specific determination

parts.quote: ‘the Determination’

tags.violation_condition: Using lowercase 'ruling' or 'determination' when referring to a specific ruling or determination

when: When referring to specific tax rulings or determinations
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Capitalisation and naming rules for subsequent mentions of tax rulings.

anchor.quote: If you use notes, cite the ATO Legal Database as the source.

covers.quote: In notes, cite the title, source and paragraph numbers

examples.note: Note citation citing ATO Legal Database

parts.quote: 4 Australian Taxation Office, Fuel Tax Determination FTD 2019/1 Fuel tax: fuel tax credits–vehicles and satisfying environmental criteria, ATO Legal Database, para [4]. [The full citation the first time; specifies the source and pinpoints paragraph 4]

tags.violation_condition: A note citation for a Tax Commissioner public ruling that omits 'ATO Legal Database' as the source

when: In notes citing Tax Commissioner public rulings
rules.why: G-4: Specifies required source in notes for ATO rulings.

anchor.quote: For pinpoint citations, use paragraph numbers for public rulings (rather than page numbers). Write the paragraph number in square brackets preceded by the words ‘para’ or ‘paras’.

covers.quote: For subsequent notes for the same public ruling, cite the number (and paragraphs for a pinpoint citation).

examples.note: Pinpoint citation using 'para [4]'

parts.quote: 4 Australian Taxation Office, Fuel Tax Determination FTD 2019/1 Fuel tax: fuel tax credits–vehicles and satisfying environmental criteria, ATO Legal Database, para [4]. [The full citation the first time; specifies the source and pinpoints paragraph 4]

examples.note: Pinpoint citation using 'paras [6]–[8]'

parts.quote: 15 FTD 2019/1, paras [6]–[8]. [Only the determination number in a subsequent note; pinpoints paragraphs 6 to 8 for the citation]

tags.violation_condition: Using page numbers instead of paragraph numbers for public rulings, or omitting 'para'/'paras' or square brackets around paragraph numbers

when: When providing pinpoint citations for public rulings in notes
rules.why: G-2, G-4: Specific format for pinpoint citations in public rulings.
